versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 28 Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.
29 Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. 30 For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”

context_lines: Jesus follows His words about revealing the Father with a personal invitation: come to Him. He addresses people who are weary and carrying burdens, and promises rest. The invitation brings the reader from hearing about His relationship with the Father to learning from Him.

He describes that learning as taking His yoke. A yoke is equipment used to harness working animals; here it pictures coming under His direction. Jesus explains the image Himself by calling people to learn from Him. Rest and discipleship belong together: the teacher who calls them is gentle and humble in heart.

The word translated easy is χρηστός, *chrēstos* (khray-STOSS). [Thayer's entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/5543.htm) gives the sense mild or manageable for the yoke in this verse, in contrast to something harsh or burdensome. The assurance concerns the kind of master Jesus is and the burden He gives. The same Gospel has already described the opposition His disciples may face.

The promise of rest for the soul recalls [Jeremiah 6:16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/jeremiah/6.htm), where God calls people to walk in His good way and find rest. Here Jesus directs the weary to Himself. He does not merely point toward relief somewhere else; He offers to give it as they come and learn.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as an invitation to receive rest from Jesus while trusting Him and learning His way. [Wesley on Matthew 11:28–30](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/) emphasizes relief from sin's guilt and power, freely given through Christ. The Catholic [Catechism, 459](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P1J.HTM), uses the invitation to learn from Jesus in explaining His role as the model for a holy life. These are complementary emphases on His saving gift and the life learned from Him.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: Rest runs through the Bible's account of God's work. [Hebrews 4:1–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/4.htm) brings together God's rest after creation, Israel's failure to enter through unbelief, and a promise still open after Joshua. It calls people to respond to God's voice in faith today.

That is a Scripture-supported connection with Jesus' invitation, rather than a claim that Hebrews is directly explaining this particular saying. Rest is more than reaching a place or stopping activity for a while; it concerns receiving what God gives and trusting Him. The same chapter then points to Jesus as the great high priest who understands human weakness and welcomes His people to receive mercy and help ([Hebrews 4:14–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/4.htm)). His gentleness here fits that larger picture of the Savior through whom people draw near to God.
